entry.heading: Chainsaw Man (Tatsuki Fujimoto)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life here is an ordinary one: food, a home, people to eat with, and the freedom to choose your own wants instead of having them chosen for you.

frames.aligns: Care for the poor; human dignity against being used as a tool; sacrificial love among friends.
frames.concerns: Gratuitous gore; sexual content and teen nudity; devil contracts as normal; cannibalism framed as "love" (ch. 96-97); suicide themes. Fantasy demons are judged by framing (CCC 2115-2117), so some parents allow it for older teens.

frames.aligns: Evil is real and deceptive; repentance-like grief; Makima as a false shepherd.
frames.concerns: Demons are taken as real, so a devil-hybrid hero and friendly devils conflict throughout; "passions" fed by sexual imagery; constant killing.

frames.aligns: Sin has consequences; manipulation is exposed; loyalty and care for a child.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence, sexual content, profanity, alcohol use by minors (many Baptists are teetotal). Views vary by congregation; Plugged In, widely used by Baptists, rated the film "Heavy" for all ages.

frames.aligns: Evil disguised as good (Makima); found family; a story some Christians use to talk about young men's brokenness (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Demonic content in a heroic frame; lust as the main motive; profanity; gore. Churches range from avoiding it to discussing it with older teens.

frames.aligns: Spiritual deception and bondage shown as real harms; freedom from control.
frames.concerns: Spiritual warfare sensitivity: devils, contracts, Hell and a hero fused with a devil are central, not incidental; sexual content; profanity.

frames.aligns: Total depravity is vivid; common grace lets some readers value its honesty about desire and abuse.
frames.concerns: Sexual imagery (WLC Q139); gore; suicide as self-murder (WLC Q136) treated as a plot twist; occult framing.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel themes: Denji cannot save himself; grace-like gifts come through others.
frames.concerns: Explicit violence and sexual content (sixth commandment); misuse of authority. LCMS and ELCA families may differ on how much to allow.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace echoes in small mercies; social holiness critique of exploitation.
frames.concerns: Holiness emphasis on purity; underage drinking against historic abstinence; profanity ("doing no harm"). Holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Imaginative tradition (C.S. Lewis) gives room for dark fantasy; critique of misused power.
frames.concerns: Chastity and gore judged case by case; occult forbidden. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ.

frames.aligns: Critique of state violence and of using people as weapons.
frames.concerns: Nonresistance: violence is the story's engine and its spectacle throughout; sexual content; profanity. Progressive Mennonites may engage it as critique; conservative groups would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, care for a child, warnings about manipulation.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth guidance against media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent" fits most chapters; alcohol (Word of Wisdom); profanity.

frames.aligns: Critique of exploited labor, poverty and state power; sympathy for an abused youth; LGBTQ side characters.
frames.concerns: Consent issues (ch. 132, 136, 167-168), sexualized teens, glorified gore; Denji's homophobia in Part 1 (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Respect for life shown through grief; critique of tyranny; truth about abuse.
frames.concerns: Orthodox: tzniut and lashon hara concerns, gore, devils; Reform: may read it as social critique with older teens. No antisemitic tropes found; Makima claims devils erased the Holocaust from history (ch. 84), a line some families may want to discuss.

frames.aligns: Mercy to orphans and animals; warnings against arrogance and control over others.
frames.concerns: Nudity and lust, alcohol, devils (shayatin) as partners and pets, mutilation of bodies, throughout.

frames.aligns: Desire and suffering; rebirth of devils; dharma-like duty in Aki.
frames.concerns: Violence against ahimsa; sexual content; the absence of the sacred. A Hindu traditionalist essay calls Denji nihilistic and Makima "desacralizing" femininity, while praising Aki and Himeno (cshc Substack).

frames.aligns: Craving as the root of suffering; impermanence; endless rebirth of devils looks like samsara (our framing).
frames.concerns: First precept: killing is constant; third precept: sexual content; appetite treated as a hero's fuel.

frames.aligns: Critique of labor exploitation, poverty and state power; Asa as an honest portrait of an awkward girl (Kotaku); platonic Denji-Power bond (Anime Feminist).
frames.concerns: Sexualization of 16-year-old characters; consent (ch. 132, 136, 167-168); Power's trauma used for Denji's growth (Anime Feminist); suicide safe-messaging.

frames.aligns: This-life meaning through friends, meals and care; no supernatural rescue; critical view of authority.
frames.concerns: Glorified gore; exploitation and consent; very little positive messaging (CSM).

frames.aligns: Strong warnings about manipulation; value of home, meals and work; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Absent and abusive fathers; crude sexuality and swearing; nihilism; cult imagery; anti-authority tone.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Pagan/occult imagery, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Hedonism (explored).

entry.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen (Gege Akutami)
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Self-giving love: Yuji, Nanami and Gojo give their lives for others. Yuji refuses to treat anyone as disposable.
frames.concerns: Curses, spirit summoning, possession and body-theft are the core power system (CCC 2115-2117 on magic and spiritism). Gore at strength 8. A cult cheers a child's death. Mei Mei / Ui Ui material. Grade reason: real concerns run through the whole series.

frames.aligns: Struggle against evil; repentance-like grief after Shibuya (ch. 127); honor for the dead.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real in Orthodox teaching, so demon-like curses and possession as a skill system weigh heavily. Constant killing, which the tradition treats as needing repentance even when justified. Grade reason: spiritual-warfare themes are inverted into tools.

frames.aligns: Responsibility after failure; courage; loyalty; Yuji's refusal to abandon others.
frames.concerns: Sorcery, summoning and spirits (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Graphic violence. Self-harm (Toji). Views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing; some families accept fantasy magic, many are cautious with spells and spirits.

frames.aligns: Clear evil fought at cost; mentors who sacrifice; the Higuruma arc read as human justice failing and grace needed (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Occult mechanics and possession; gore; despair. Range is wide: some churches treat the magic like Tolkien-style fantasy, others avoid spirit-contact stories entirely.

frames.aligns: Courage and self-sacrifice; evil is real and must be fought.
frames.concerns: Curses, possession, body-stealing and summoned spirits are the engine of the entire story, which the tradition's spiritual-warfare teaching treats as dangerous even in fiction. Demon-like villains are fan favorites. Grade reason: conflicts with core teaching throughout.

frames.aligns: Total depravity is vivid: every institution and most adults fail. Common grace: self-sacrifice and loyalty still shine.
frames.concerns: Occult framework; gore; suicide (WLC Q136 calls it self-murder, handled pastorally).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: the story is heavy on law (judgment, guilt, Higuruma's court) and shows grace mainly as forgiveness between brothers (Yuji and Choso).
frames.concerns: Occult themes (Large Catechism on misuse of God's name includes sorcery); graphic violence. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace-like moments: Yuji keeps choosing to help after failing. Social holiness: reform of an unjust system.
frames.concerns: Occult; violence; holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Sacrifice and duty; grief and remembrance; fantasy has deep Anglican roots (C.S. Lewis).
frames.concerns: Occult system; gore. Episcopal families generally less concerned than ACNA families.

frames.aligns: Mutual care; refusal to treat anyone as disposable.
frames.concerns: Nonresistance (Matthew 5:39): the series is built on heroic violence. Occult themes. Conservative groups avoid much fantasy media. Mennonite Church USA families are more varied. Grade reason: conflicts with core teaching throughout.

frames.aligns: Family-like loyalty; sacrifice; repentance after failure.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth (2022) warns against media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent"; the violence and horror are central. Occult and spirit contact. Mei Mei material.

frames.aligns: Justice themes: corrupt elders, a failed court (Higuruma), inherited privilege, Maki against a sexist clan.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; critics' view that women are sidelined (ANN review); Mei Mei material and consent.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh-like ethic: Yuji acts to save lives. Memory of the dead is central.
frames.concerns: Sorcery is forbidden (Deuteronomy 18), though many liberal Jewish families accept fantasy. Gore; suicide. Orthodox families likely grade lower (D).

frames.aligns: Courage, protecting the weak, patience (sabr), justice against corrupt elders.
frames.concerns: Sihr (sorcery) and spirit summoning are the core mechanic. Possession and body-theft. Graphic killing. Brief immodesty and the Mei Mei material.

frames.aligns: Dharma-like duty to fight to protect others; karma-like consequences for cruelty.
frames.concerns: Ahimsa versus constant killing; Buddhist and folk imagery used for combat.

frames.aligns: Many Buddhist motifs: suffering born of negative emotion (curses), impermanence, mudras, "I alone am the honored one." Yuji's acceptance that he is one part of a larger whole.
frames.concerns: Buddhist imagery is used for battle and spectacle; the "honored one" phrase is spoken in pride. The first precept (non-harm) is rarely discussed.

frames.aligns: Critique of a closed, aging elite and inherited privilege; Maki against a misogynist clan; Higuruma's critique of the courts.
frames.concerns: Critics argue women are sidelined in the second half (Nobara absent from ch. 125 to ch. 267). Mei Mei / Ui Ui framing and consent. Suicide shown on page (safe-messaging concern).

frames.aligns: Yuji's ethic rests on human dignity and care, not divine command; the strongest and the cruelest lose to cooperation. Magic is clearly fiction.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence and gore; despair and suicide content for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Duty, sacrifice, loyalty, honor, respect for good mentors (Nanami, Yaga). Clear villains. Responsibility for consequences.
frames.concerns: Authority and tradition are almost always shown as corrupt. Occult content. Gore and despair. Fan culture celebrating Sukuna.

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist) imagery, Pagan/occult (Japanese folk religion), Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Nihilism (critiqued). The labels below are this entry's framing unless a source is named.

entry.heading: Berserk
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a stubborn struggle: you keep fighting against fate, cruelty and your own rage, and you choose to protect the people beside you rather than sacrifice them for a dream.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual violence shown as atrocity with lasting consequences; critics dispute how it is drawn

frames.aligns: Dignity of victims; Guts's turn from vengeance to protection; the cost of pride (Griffith).
frames.concerns: Explicit rape and nudity (chastity and modesty, CCC 2354 on pornographic depiction, 2521-2524); gratuitous violence; demonic pact as central plot; the Holy See and inquisition shown as cruel, which some Catholics read as aimed at the Church.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions; Guts's "inner beast" as a picture of rage.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real in the tradition, so demonic sacrifice and a god of evil are a serious concern; explicit sexual imagery against chastity; killing and torture constant (St. Basil, canon 13).

frames.aligns: Clear evil in the God Hand; fellowship and protection in the later arcs.
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual content and rape; occult and witchcraft shown positively (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); constant gore; profanity. Each congregation is self-governing, so some adult Baptists read it, but most families would not give it to a teen.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Guts's arc as moving toward "restored faith instead of bitter distrust" and fellowship (Hebrews 12:24).
frames.concerns: Graphic rape and gore weighed by purpose; positive witchcraft; a corrupt church; demonic pacts.

frames.aligns: Spiritual warfare imagery: a real fight against demonic powers.
frames.concerns: Spiritual warfare is central to this tradition, so demonic sacrifice, cursed brands, witchcraft taught as good and spirit contact are a significant concern even in fiction; explicit sexual content.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has a strong echo: human sin produces the Idea of Evil and the apostles. Common grace allows adults to value serious art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual imagery (WLC Q139); gore; a fatalistic "causality" in place of providence; the church shown as cruel.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: no character can save himself; the story shows the bondage of the will.
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual content (sixth commandment); gore; witchcraft; demonic pacts. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Holiness of care: the later arcs center caring for a wounded woman.
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual violence; gore; occult. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Strong tradition of dark fantasy and moral seriousness (Lewis, Tolkien); just-war themes.
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual violence and nudity; gore. Content judged case by case; Episcopal and ACNA families both likely to see this as adult reading.

frames.aligns: Mercy toward the wounded; a small caring community.
frames.concerns: Nonresistance (Matthew 5:39): violence and revenge are the main engine of the story; sexual content; separation from worldly media.

frames.aligns: Family-like loyalty; healing from trauma.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks youth to avoid media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent"; Berserk is all three at a strong level; the publisher rates it 18+. Members vary in strictness, but this is outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Critique of religious violence and fanaticism (Mozgus, witch hunts); empathy for refugees and the poor; Casca's recovery through women's care.
frames.concerns: Gratuitous sexual violence; the "fridging" of Casca; Guts as a male abuse survivor needs careful handling; glorified violence.

frames.aligns: Respect for life amid chaos; memory of the dead (the Band); critique of inquisitions and witch hunts, which echo historical persecution.
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual content (tzniut; strongest concern in Orthodox homes); gore; sorcery (Deuteronomy 18); a cosmic god of evil.

frames.aligns: Patience under trial (sabr); loyalty; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual content and nudity (haya); sorcery shown positively (sihr); demonic beings worshipped and given power; constant violence; the series is plainly outside Muslim media norms for youth.

frames.aligns: Karma-like "causality"; the duty to protect; Ganishka transforms into a figure the story calls Shiva (Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual content; gore; use of a Hindu deity's name for a monstrous form may concern some. Communities vary.

frames.aligns: Suffering, craving and attachment (Griffith's dream, the apostles' trades); the Idea of Evil as born from human minds.
frames.concerns: Killing and sexual misconduct shown in extreme detail (first and third precepts); revenge as motive.

frames.aligns: Critique of religious fanaticism and abusive power; the long trauma-recovery arc; a male survivor of child sexual abuse.
frames.concerns: Gratuitous and frequent sexual violence (MyAnimeList reviewers; Anime Feminist; The Comics Journal); Casca's silence for 27 volumes; racial depiction debates; safe-messaging on suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: Human will against an indifferent or hostile cosmos; friendship and care as what gives life meaning; critique of superstition and inquisition.
frames.concerns: Gratuitous sexual violence; gore; the supernatural is fiction. Adult reading by the publisher's rating.

frames.aligns: Courage, endurance, protective masculinity in Guts's later arcs, loyalty and honor (Zodd, the Skull Knight).
frames.concerns: Explicit sexual content; gore; occult; a corrupt church; anti-authority themes. Some conservative commentators praise Guts as a masculine model (Substack essays found, not opened).

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Pagan/occult (explored), Nihilism (explored and resisted), Christian (critiqued as institution, echoed in themes).

entry.heading: One Piece
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a free life spent chasing your own dream, side by side with friends who would die for you, and never bowing to anyone who claims the right to own other people.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; condemned when villains do it
Played as comedy; sexual coercion condemned

content.raw: 3 (manga); higher in the anime dub and live action

content.framing: Alcohol and tobacco shown casually; drugs condemned

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person; condemnation of slavery and of rulers who make themselves gods; self-giving love (Ace, Kuma, Oden). A Pauline.org reviewer reads Luffy's rescue of Nami as an image of Christ seeking the lost.
frames.concerns: Fan service and leering played for laughs (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty); constant drinking and smoking; violence as the default answer. Grade reason: strong moral core, but recurring immodesty and harassment gags.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for friends; false gods humbled; mercy (Luffy rarely kills).
frames.concerns: Sexual imagery feeds the "passions"; killing and war shown as heroic (St. Basil, canon 13); a human made into a "sun god"; undead. Grade reason: real concerns on both modesty and spiritual imagery.

frames.aligns: Clear good versus evil; courage; freeing the enslaved; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Fan service (purity emphasis); heroes drink and smoke (SBC resolutions urge abstinence); the Nika "god" identity; gender-variant characters (BF&M 2000, Article XVIII). Grade reason: real concerns, and views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles, an evangelical anime site, reads Luffy's freedom as a picture of "freedom through a Savior" ([BTT](https://beneaththetangles.com/2021/05/06/one-piece-stirs-a-call-to-freedom-a-call-to-adventure)). Rebellion against evil rulers is admired.
frames.concerns: Plugged In (live action) warns of "content that lurks below these waves": blood, a man sliced in half, profanity, transgender characters, objectified women ([Plugged In](https://www.pluggedin.com/tv-reviews/one-piece/)). Grade reason: positive themes, mixed review from the tradition's main media guide.

frames.aligns: Liberation of captives (Luke 4:18 resonance); loyalty; false gods unmasked.
frames.concerns: Spiritual-warfare sensitivity: a human awakened as a "Sun God", Haki as "spiritual energy" (Plugged In), zombies and shadow-theft (Thriller Bark), cursed swords; alcohol (many abstain); sexualized art. Grade reason: several holiness and occult concerns at once.

frames.aligns: Total depravity on display: power corrupts every unchecked ruler; common grace in a non-Christian story's hatred of slavery.
frames.concerns: Sexual imagery (WLC Q139); heroes' drunkenness; outlaws as heroes against the magistrate (WLC Q123-133). Grade reason: common-grace reading fits, with commandment-level concerns.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: the story's worst villains abuse the sword the state holds; grace-like forgiveness of defeated foes.
frames.concerns: Fan service (sixth commandment explanation); outlaw heroes against authority (fourth commandment); drinking. LCMS and ELCA families differ on gender-variant characters. Grade reason: themes discussable; modesty concerns recur.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: freeing slaves, fighting racism (Fish-Man Island); characters growing toward goodness.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and tobacco (holiness bodies ask members to abstain); fan service; heroic violence. UMC and Global Methodist families differ on gender themes. Grade reason: justice themes fit; personal-holiness concerns recur.

frames.aligns: Fantasy and myth sit comfortably in the tradition (C.S. Lewis); anti-slavery and anti-tyranny themes; found family.
frames.concerns: Fan service and harassment gags; drunkenness. Episcopal and ACNA families differ on gender-variant characters. Grade reason: broad fit; content judged case by case.

frames.aligns: Suspicion of state power; Luffy's refusal to rule the islands he frees; care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Violence is the main way every arc ends; heroes are fighters; drinking; immodest dress. Many conservative families avoid such media altogether. Grade reason: nonresistance conflicts with the premise.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, keeping promises, self-sacrifice; family-like bonds.
frames.concerns: Constant alcohol and tobacco (Word of Wisdom); immodest designs and harassment gags; violence. For the Strength of Youth (2022) asks youth to choose media that is not "vulgar, immoral, violent". Grade reason: several standards touched in most arcs.

frames.aligns: Social-justice core: slavery, racism, aristocracy, erasure of history; gender-variant characters shown with acceptance (CSM).
frames.concerns: Exploitative fan service and harassment played as comedy; okama characters sometimes used for laughs. Grade reason: themes align; representation and consent are the concerns.

frames.aligns: An Exodus-like hatred of slavery and of rulers who call themselves gods; memory against erased history (Ohara); dignity of the stranger (fish-men).
frames.concerns: Tzniut concerns over fan service (strongest in Orthodox homes); a man worshipped as a god; heroic violence. Grade reason: themes fit; views vary across movements.

frames.aligns: Justice ('adl) against oppressors; freeing slaves as a virtue (Qur'an 90:13); hospitality and keeping promises.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and tobacco everywhere (Qur'an 5:90); immodest clothing and leering (haya); a man revered as a "sun god" touches on shirk; gender-variant characters. Grade reason: several clear prohibitions recur.

frames.aligns: Dharma as duty to protect the weak; loyalty to a rightful lord (Wano's retainers to Oden); a righteous war against tyrants (Gita).
frames.concerns: Intoxicants; fan service; ahimsa strained by constant fighting. Grade reason: duty theme fits, with modesty and non-harm notes.

frames.aligns: Compassion for suffering beings; letting go of hatred (Hody's revenge rejected); impermanence of power.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main way problems end (first precept); intoxicants (fifth precept); ambition ("King of the Pirates") as a life goal. Grade reason: themes fit, conduct conflicts.

frames.aligns: Anti-slavery, anti-racism, anti-aristocracy; gender-variant characters shown kindly (CSM); found family.
frames.concerns: Sexualized female designs and harassment gags; okama as comic relief; Anime Feminist's essay argues Oda answered female critics by sexualizing women more ([Anime Feminist](https://animefeminist.com/choosing-toremain-strong-against-female-criticism-the-vindictive-storytelling-of-oda-eiichiro)). Grade reason: themes align, with real representation and consent concerns.

frames.aligns: Human solidarity and inherited will carry meaning; no god rewards virtue; knowledge defended against censorship (Ohara).
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; exploitation in fan service; Nika as a "god", though shown as myth inside fiction. Grade reason: close to the series' human-centered ethics, with exploitation concerns.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honor, duty, gratitude; strong fathers and mentors; good monarchs honored; courage against tyranny.
frames.concerns: Outlaws as heroes and distrust of all government; fan service; gender-identity themes (Ivankov, Yamato) and how adaptations localize them (Bounding Into Comics on "New Trans"). Grade reason: traditional virtues, anti-authority premise.

lenses.label: Might makes right
lenses.stance: Critiqued, though power decides most fights

entry.dominant: Libertarianism (liberty and anti-authoritarianism), Classical virtue ethics (loyalty and courage), Communitarianism (the crew and freed peoples), and a critique of Collectivism/authoritarianism. "Anti-authoritarian" is drawn from Wikipedia's account of the themes. The labels Critical theory, Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Pragmatism and Confucian ethics are our framing, not any source's.

entry.heading: Attack on Titan (Shingeki no Kyojin)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived freely and for the people you love, but freedom pursued through violence spreads the hatred it means to escape; the story asks the reader to keep looking for understanding even when the world is cruel.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for friends; the dignity of the enemy shown from inside Marley; forgiveness (the Blouse family toward Gabi). Grade reason: real moral seriousness, but gore and a genocidal hero dominate.
frames.concerns: Gratuitous-looking gore; the hero's genocide; a suicide attempt (CCC 2280-2283); a "devil" origin myth. Little sexual content.

frames.aligns: Repentance as a long road (Reiner, Gabi); the burden of killing even in war. Grade reason: themes of repentance fit, but violence and demonic imagery are heavy.
frames.concerns: St. Basil's canon 13 treats killing in war as needing repentance; here killing is constant. "Devil" pact imagery may be a serious concern where evil spirits are taken as real.

frames.aligns: Clear picture of sin passed down and of human evil; sacrifice for others. Grade reason: graphic violence and profanity are common concerns. Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence (a common concern); some profanity in the English text; revenge as motive (Romans 12:19); "devil" pact as myth.

frames.aligns: Christian writers draw out (Thirst.sg and Christ and Pop Culture titles; not opened) sin, sacrifice and overcoming evil with good. Grade reason: violence weighed by purpose; many will find the purpose serious but the level too high for younger teens.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; a hero who becomes a mass killer; nihilistic voices (Kenny, Zeke).

frames.aligns: Longing for freedom and deliverance; forgiveness. Grade reason: spiritual-warfare sensitivity makes the occult-flavored origin a larger concern here than in other Christian rows.
frames.concerns: Power from a pact with a "devil" (ch. 122); Paths and a spirit world binding a people; graphic violence.

frames.aligns: Realism about total depravity: no one is innocent, including the heroes. Common grace lets readers value the art and its questions. Grade reason: worldview fit is strong; violence remains a real concern.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; protagonist's genocide; a suicide attempt (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Two-kingdoms questions: governments lie and wage war, yet order matters. Law exposes guilt (Reiner, Gabi). Grade reason: rich for law-and-gospel discussion; violence a concern.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; little gospel (forgiveness is human, not divine). LCMS and ELCA families may weigh this differently.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace glimpsed in former enemies changing (Gabi, Reiner); social holiness against ethnic hatred. Grade reason: holiness emphasis and strong peace emphasis in many churches make the violence a significant concern.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; profanity; hero's genocide. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just-war tradition (Article 37) fits the story's questions; forgiveness of enemies. Grade reason: fit with discussion; Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on the gender questions.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; hero's genocide; suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: The story's anti-war ending; violence shown as a cycle that corrupts everyone. Grade reason: the critique of violence fits, but violence is the story's constant subject and spectacle. Old Order and conservative groups would likely treat it as F; MC USA families may read it as an anti-war text.
frames.concerns: Nonresistance (Matthew 5:39): nearly every conflict is solved by force; children trained as soldiers.

frames.aligns: Courage, sacrifice and family love; repentance of former enemies. Grade reason: For the Strength of Youth asks youth to avoid media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent," and the violence is constant.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; profanity; spiked wine (Word of Wisdom); suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: Peace-and-justice reading: a critique of ethnonationalism, propaganda and dehumanization; anti-war ending. Grade reason: strong thematic fit; the Holocaust-imagery debate and glorified-violence concern need discussion.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; critics' concern that Holocaust imagery is used carelessly (New Republic, JTA); a female lead centered on a man.

frames.aligns: Memory of persecution and the cost of dehumanization; self-defense debated; respect for life. Grade reason: views are split on whether the Eldian story honors or distorts Holocaust memory.
frames.concerns: Armbands, internment zones and a "euthanasia" plan echo the Holocaust (ch. 86-88, 114). Some Jewish fans quoted by JTA and critics see antisemitic tropes (Eldians as a "devil" people whose blood carries power); others read it as a sympathetic allegory of persecution.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; courage; the horror of killing innocents is not hidden. Grade reason: mass killing of civilians by the hero and constant gore are serious concerns.
frames.concerns: Killing innocents; spiked wine; suicide attempt (forbidden); a "devil" pact as source of power. Titan nudity is non-sexual.

frames.aligns: Dharma and righteous war are central questions; karma-like cycles of action and consequence across generations. Grade reason: invites Gita-style discussion; ahimsa and graphic violence a concern.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; children as soldiers; disrespect to parents is shown as costly.

frames.aligns: The cycle of hatred and revenge is the core theme; attachment and fear drive suffering. Grade reason: close thematic fit; first-precept concern with constant killing.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; despair; suicide attempt; spiked wine (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Critique of ethnonationalism, propaganda and dehumanization; women soldiers as equals; anti-war ending. Grade reason: themes fit, but critics on the left are split on whether the story undercuts its own anti-fascism.

entry.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived for others. You protect the weak, honor the dead, keep promises, and pass your will to the next generation. A long or powerful life bought by harming others is worth nothing.

frames.aligns: Self-giving love and mercy toward the repentant; honor for parents and the dead.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; Kagaya's self-detonation and other suicide-adjacent scenes (CCC 2280-2283); Buddhist and Shinto afterlife imagery judged by how it is framed.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions (Muzan's craving, Kokushibo's envy); repentance at death (Akaza, ch. 156); prayer-like care for the dead.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real in the tradition, so the demon imagery is a real concern for some families; killing, even when just, calls for repentance (St. Basil); non-Christian afterlife scenes.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; sacrifice for others; honoring parents (Ephesians 6:1).
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; Buddhist and Shinto spirituality shown as real (John 14:6); cleavage and red-light district setting. Views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Redemption themes; Equip.org highlights compassion: "Humanizing is the goal, instead of demonizing," and links it to Romans 2:4.
frames.concerns: Gore ("It's not for kids," Equip.org); non-Christian afterlife and spirituality; occasional fan service.

frames.aligns: Clear spiritual battle between good and evil; courage and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Spiritual warfare is central to this tradition, so literal demons, spirit encounters, ritual fire-god dance and a demon-led cult are often a significant concern even in fiction. Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: demons are humans whose sin has grown monstrous. Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; suicide-adjacent scenes (WLC Q136 on self-murder); other religions' afterlife shown as real.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: the Corps bears the sword to protect the weak, like lawful authority. Law and gospel: demons cannot save themselves; mercy comes from outside them.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; non-Christian spirituality. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Holiness of life and works of mercy; prevenient grace has an echo in demons who remember their humanity at the end.
frames.concerns: Violence (the UMC's peace emphasis); suicide-adjacent scenes; some fan service. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) usually more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just war (Article 37) fits the Corps' fight; a strong tradition of fantasy literature (C.S. Lewis).
frames.concerns: Violence; suicide-adjacent scenes. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender, not on this content.

frames.aligns: Humility, compassion for enemies, community care.
frames.concerns: Nonresistance (Matthew 5:39): violence is the heroes' main tool and is shown as heroic throughout. Conservative groups avoid much fantasy media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as central and eternal; reunion with loved ones after death; service and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks youth to avoid media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent"; the gore is the main issue, with fan service second. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the marginalized: demon backstories trace harm to poverty and abuse (ch. 96, 154).
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; traditional gender roles; Nezuko's limited voice; the Rising Sun dispute and Korean historical sensitivities.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and its protection; honoring parents (Exodus 20:12); memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; suicide-adjacent scenes (traditionally forbidden, treated with compassion today); modesty concerns weigh more in Orthodox homes than Reform ones.

frames.aligns: Family loyalty, care for a sister, patience (sabr), fighting only to stop oppression, forgiveness preferred.
frames.concerns: Violence; revealing outfits and red-light setting (haya); polytheistic ritual and afterlife imagery; self-destruction scenes, read against the prohibition of suicide (Qur'an 4:29).

frames.aligns: Dharma may require righteous fighting (Bhagavad Gita); family duty and respect for elders; karma and rebirth (ch. 205).
frames.concerns: Graphic violence against ahimsa ideals; some modesty concerns. Few religious conflicts.

frames.aligns: Draws on Buddhist ideas: craving (Muzan), compassion for all beings, impermanence, a monk-warrior (Gyomei), rebirth (ch. 205).
frames.concerns: Killing is central to the plot, against the first precept; demons are destroyed rather than released. Japanese schools may see the imagery as familiar; others less so.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the marginalized; harm traced to poverty and abuse; critique of rule by fear.
frames.concerns: Mostly traditional gender roles; Nezuko's silence and adult-form design (Anime Feminist; The Mary Sue); Mitsuri's uniform gag; polygamy played lightly; Korean historical sensitivities; suicide portrayal.

frames.aligns: Human bonds and the value of a finite life over endless demon life (Kagaya: human thoughts endure, ch. 137); reason and empathy.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; suicide-adjacent scenes need mental-health framing; afterlife scenes as fiction.

frames.aligns: Duty, honor, sacrifice, respect for elders, protective masculinity. The Federalist praises its "courage, family, strength, and masculine virtue."
frames.concerns: Intense gore; for some religious conservatives, demonic and occult imagery; comic cross-dressing; red-light district arc.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics, Communitarianism, Dharmic (Buddhist), Traditionalism, Stoicism.

entry.title: Tokyo Ghoul
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In an alternate Tokyo, ghouls who look human but must eat human flesh live in secret. University student Ken Kaneki survives a ghoul attack and is surgically turned into a half-ghoul, then learns to survive among ghouls at the cafe Anteiku while hiding his condition from his human friends. The story follows his struggle to keep his humanity amid conflict with the ghoul-hunting CCG.
entry.life_message: It holds up keeping one's humanity and care for others when the world forces a choice between two hostile sides.

His outgoing classmate Marin Kitagawa discovers his skill and asks him to make her cosplay costumes, and their collaboration grows into a romance that, per Wikipedia, ends in marriage and a daughter.
entry.life_message: Holds up loving your craft and your interests openly, and finding people who accept you as you are.

entry.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story shows a life spent claiming the power to judge others, and lets the reader watch where that leads. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

content.frequency: Constant (deaths every few chapters), mostly non-graphic

frames.aligns: The ruin of a proud man who makes himself judge of life and death; the innocent suffer from his "justice"; due process upheld in the end.
frames.concerns: Mass killing told in a stylish way; suicides dictated by the notebook (CCC 2280-2283); death gods; the "Mu" rule denies judgment and afterlife. Many parishes would treat it as older-teen reading.

frames.aligns: Light reads as a picture of the passions, above all pride, and of a man refusing repentance; an Orthodox writer at Geeks Under Grace reads it as "the throne without the Cross."
frames.concerns: Death gods taken seriously as spirits can be a concern where evil spirits are held to be real; killing even of criminals calls for repentance in the tradition; no hope of resurrection in the story's rules.

frames.aligns: Clear arc from sin to ruin; deception is exposed; a thoughtful teen can discuss justice and the death penalty.
frames.concerns: Graphic-enough violence, coerced suicide, death gods and a human claiming divinity; profanity in the Viz text. Views on entertainment vary by congregation, as each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Plugged In praises the "compelling plot" and "conversations on morality and justice"; Christian reviewers read Light as a man seizing God's throne.
frames.concerns: Plugged In warns of "spiritual themes, violence, and language" and apple and Eden imagery (anime). Range is broad, from Bible churches that skip it to churches that use it for worldview talks.

frames.aligns: The story punishes the man who takes a death god's power.
frames.concerns: Spiritual warfare is central to the tradition: a supernatural death god who gives a human power to kill, and a notebook that works like a curse, can be a significant concern even as fiction.

frames.aligns: Light can be read as a study in total depravity: a gifted, "good" student whose heart turns to self-worship; through common grace, a non-Christian story still tells truth about sin.
frames.concerns: Many deaths, coerced suicides (self-murder, WLC Q136) and constant lying by the protagonist.

frames.aligns: A two-kingdoms reading fits: God works through lawful authority (police, courts), and Light usurps it; law exposes him in the end.
frames.concerns: Violence, suicides and death gods; Light breaks the fourth and fifth commandments. LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Holiness and "do no harm" set against a man who does harm for "good"; Soichiro's integrity.
frames.concerns: Violence, coerced suicide and profanity; holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) may be stricter than UMC families.

frames.aligns: Fits a tradition with deep roots in moral fantasy and crime fiction; just-war and lawful-authority teaching (Article 37) frame the duel.
frames.concerns: Many deaths and suicides; death gods. ACNA families may be more cautious than Episcopal families.

frames.aligns: Shows violence and the will to punish as a trap that consumes the one who uses it.
frames.concerns: Pacifism and nonresistance (Matthew 5:39) mean a story built on killing, police shoot-outs and deception is often a significant concern; conservative groups avoid such media, while MC USA families may read it as a critique of the death penalty.

frames.aligns: Agency and its consequences; honesty (Article of Faith 13) shown as what finally defeats a liar.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks youth to avoid media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent"; mass killing, coerced suicide and profanity weigh on that. Families vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: A sharp critique of the death penalty, vigilantism, surveillance and populist media fits the tradition's peace-and-justice focus.
frames.concerns: Women defined by love for Light (AnimeFeminist); suicides need mental-health framing; violence.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and due process; the danger of a man who makes himself an idol. Orthodox families may be more cautious than Reform families.
frames.concerns: Taking life outside lawful courts; suicide (traditionally forbidden); a human claiming godhood.

frames.aligns: Strong theme that unjust killing is grave and arrogance (kibr) leads to ruin.
frames.concerns: Killing by private judgment; a human calling himself god (a form of shirk in Islamic terms); suicide (forbidden); denial of afterlife and judgment at the end.

frames.aligns: Karma-like return: Light's actions bring his own end; satya (truth) defeats deception.
frames.concerns: Many deaths; ahimsa (non-harm); suicide discouraged; respect for parents broken by Light.

frames.aligns: Karma-like logic; attachment to power and self drives suffering; Ryuk's detachment echoes impermanence.
frames.concerns: Many deaths (first precept); constant false speech (fourth precept); the "Mu" ending can read as nihilism rather than Buddhist emptiness, though "mu" is also a Zen term.

frames.aligns: A sharp critique of vigilante "justice," the death penalty, mass surveillance and populist media.
frames.concerns: Flat female characters (AnimeFeminist); suicides shown without safe-messaging framing; police torture-like methods shown as clever; no LGBTQ+ characters (CSM).

frames.aligns: Reason, evidence and due process win; human life defended without religious grounding; no supernatural rescue.
frames.concerns: Glamor of a clever killer; violence and suicides for younger teens.

frames.aligns: Law and order matter; the police and a good father (Soichiro) are honorable; evil is defeated in the end.
frames.concerns: Glamor of a teen serial killer; Light deceives his father and endangers his family; the story's ambiguity about justice.

entry.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued), Nihilism (explored), Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored, mostly as imagery and structure), Existentialism (explored).

entry.heading: Naruto (Masashi Kishimoto, 1999-2014)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you never give up, earn the recognition of others through effort and loyalty, and break cycles of hatred by understanding and forgiving even your enemies.

frames.aligns: Love of enemies and redemption of villains (Gaara, Nagato, Obito); an outcast child's dignity; self-gift for friends. Fantasy powers are framed as story mechanics, which the tradition often tolerates.
frames.concerns: Comic nudity and voyeurism; Shinto and Buddhist powers and spirit summoning; necromancy-like reanimation; suicide in backstories (Sakumo; Yashamaru's attack on Gaara).

frames.aligns: Forgiveness of enemies and repentance of villains echo the call to theosis (growth toward God through repentance). Self-sacrifice for friends.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real in the tradition, so a demon fox sealed in a child, spirit summoning, reanimated dead and a death-god cult read as more than fantasy for many families. Constant killing, which the tradition holds calls for repentance even in war. Sexual gags and "passions." Stricter parishes may weigh this as Significant.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, loyalty, a hero who refuses revenge (Romans 12:19). Grace-like acceptance of an outcast (Beneath the Tangles reads Iruka's acceptance through Ephesians 2).
frames.concerns: Spells, summoning and spirits are where many Baptist families are cautious (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Nudity gags and a peeping mentor. Tsunade's drinking played for laughs, a concern for the many teetotal Baptists.

frames.aligns: Servant leadership, grace before merit, forgiveness of enemies (Beneath the Tangles). Many evangelicals accept Tolkien/Lewis-style fantasy magic.
frames.concerns: Chakra, summoning and reanimating the dead may read as spirit contact rather than Tolkien-style magic. Fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, and a hero who will not take revenge.
frames.concerns: Spiritual warfare is central in this tradition. A demon-like beast sealed in a child, the Jashin blood ritual, spirit summoning and reanimation of the dead are often a significant concern even in fiction. Sexual gags and alcohol.

frames.aligns: Common grace in culture: a non-Christian work can show real goods such as sacrifice and forgiveness. Every main character is flawed, which fits the doctrine of total depravity; villains are not simply monsters.
frames.concerns: Occult imagery; vengeance as a long motive; sexual gags (WLC Q139). Sakumo's suicide (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: Naruto cannot earn acceptance by effort alone; it comes first from Iruka, then others. Two kingdoms: the village's rulers bear a sword and can abuse it (Danzo).
frames.concerns: Fantasy occult elements (usually accepted as fiction in LCMS/ELCA practice, with care); comic nudity.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace: an outcast is loved before he changes. Social holiness: the story challenges clan discrimination and secret violence. Strong peace theme.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) ask members to abstain from alcohol, so Tsunade's drinking may concern them more than UMC families. Comic nudity.

frames.aligns: The tradition has deep roots in fantasy literature (C.S. Lewis). Forgiveness, sacrifice, reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Comic nudity; occult-flavored powers, judged case by case.

frames.aligns: The central claim, that revenge must end and enemies be understood, is close to the tradition's nonresistance.
frames.concerns: Yet nearly every conflict is settled by combat, and fighting is heroic. Conservative groups avoid much fantasy media and value separation from "the world." Sexual gags.

frames.aligns: Family and sacrifice; forgiveness; respect for teachers; the ending's marriages and children.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth (2022) asks youth to avoid media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent." Nudity gags, alcohol and constant violence fall there. Spirit contact.

frames.aligns: Social justice: criticism of war, clan discrimination, secret police and child soldiers; reconciliation with enemies.
frames.concerns: Gender roles (women as healers and wives), the Killer Bee stereotype CSM flags, fat jokes, and a sexual-harassment gag culture (Jiraiya).

frames.aligns: Respect for life, teachers and parents (Exodus 20:12); breaking cycles of revenge.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and spirit summoning (Deuteronomy 18), more of a concern in Orthodox homes than Reform ones. Tzniut (modesty) and the nudity gags. Lashon hara-like mocking (fat jokes).

frames.aligns: Mercy, patience (sabr), care for orphans (Qur'an 93:9), keeping promises, forgiveness over revenge (42:40).
frames.concerns: Alcohol and gambling played for laughs (5:90). Sihr and spirit summoning (2:102). Many named gods (Shinto deities as technique names), which some read as shirk imagery. Nudity gags against haya (modesty).

frames.aligns: Karma-like chains of cause and effect, rebirth (Indra and Ashura's souls), chakra as life energy, and dharma as duty to community.
frames.concerns: Hindu names (Indra, Ashura/asura, chakra) used loosely in a fighting story; some may see careless use of sacred terms. Alcohol.

frames.aligns: The "cycle of hatred" mirrors the teaching that hatred is not ended by hatred. Pain's six bodies are named for the six realms. Naruto's choice not to take revenge.
frames.concerns: Buddhist terms used as names of weapons and a villain's bodies. Frequent violence (first precept). Intoxicants played for laughs (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: An outcast's dignity, empathy for enemies, criticism of war, secret police and clan discrimination.
frames.concerns: CSM flags sexism, fatphobia, disability clichés and the Killer Bee stereotype. Child soldiers as normal. Women end as wives and mothers (ch. 699-700). Sexual-harassment humor.

frames.aligns: Peace comes from people understanding each other, with no god intervening; reason and empathy defeat ideology (Pain, Madara).
frames.concerns: Destiny and bloodline (the reincarnation reveal) cut against self-made achievement. Violence glorified in fight scenes.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty to community, respect for teachers and elders, courage, inherited "Will of Fire," marriage and children at the end.
frames.concerns: Crude humor and nudity gags; a "pervert" mentor shown as wise; drinking and gambling; a hero who defies superiors.

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (village and "Will of Fire"), Dharmic (Buddhist cycle of hatred), Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics. Lens labels are this entry's framing unless a source is named. Wikipedia's Naruto article notes Confucian values (respect for teachers, filial duty, group over self); the other labels are this entry's own.

entry.title: A Silent Voice
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In elementary school, Shoya Ishida leads the bullying of Shoko Nishimiya, a deaf transfer student, until his classmates turn on him and he is isolated for years. As a suicidal high schooler he seeks her out to make amends, and the story follows both of them and their former classmates as they face guilt, depression and the hard work of reconciliation.
entry.life_message: Holds up facing the harm you have done, making amends, and learning to forgive yourself and live with others.

entry.heading: Dragon Ball (manga, 1984-1995)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one of joyful striving: train hard, keep getting stronger, enjoy the fight, protect your friends, forgive rivals and give former enemies a place at the table.

content.frequency: Constant in the second half; frequent in the first
content.framing: Endorsed (fighting as virtue), with deaths shown with consequences
Played for laughs; Roshi's lechery is mocked but rarely punished

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for others; mercy to enemies; conversion of villains; fidelity of friends. Grade reason: real virtues, mixed with modesty and religious concerns.
frames.concerns: Polytheistic gods as fighters; resurrection by wish rather than grace; lechery and child-nudity gags (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Repentance and transformation of enemies (Piccolo, Vegeta); self-sacrifice. Grade reason: transformation theme fits; spiritual imagery concerns.
frames.concerns: A "Demon King," demon-realm figures and a wizard (Babidi) may read as demonic imagery; fighting as joy (the tradition treats killing as needing repentance, St. Basil canon 13); "passions" in the sexual gags.

frames.aligns: Courage, perseverance, loyalty, redemption arcs. Grade reason: real concerns; views vary by congregation.
frames.concerns: Other gods shown as real (John 14:6); sexual gags and nudity, often a major concern; drinking played for laughs, where many are teetotal. Many families would treat vols. 1-16 as Significant.

frames.aligns: Friendship, teamwork and sacrifice (Beneath the Tangles). Grade reason: watchable with discernment, per the tradition's own reviewers.
frames.concerns: Beneath the Tangles: the series reinforces Japanese spiritual ideas; "Animism, reincarnation, and the such are part of life" in its world; answers "both yes and no." Movieguide (on the 2014 Battle of Gods film, not the manga) calls the worldview "very strong polytheistic pagan."

frames.aligns: Courage, protecting the weak, redemption. Grade reason: spiritual-warfare concerns run through the cosmology.
frames.concerns: Many gods, a Demon King, wizards, magic orbs and an afterlife without one God may be seen as spiritually real and dangerous; sexual humor (holiness standards); drinking. Plugged In warns of "dark and disturbing spiritual fascinations."

frames.aligns: Common grace: real goodness (loyalty, sacrifice) in a non-Christian story. Grade reason: common-grace reading fits, with first- and seventh-commandment concerns.
frames.concerns: False gods as characters; sexual imagery (WLC Q139); might as the final arbiter.

frames.aligns: Fantasy is often accepted; mercy and forgiveness of enemies. Grade reason: fantasy accepted; sexual gags and gods still raise questions.
frames.concerns: Gods surpassed by training (salvation by effort); sexual gags (sixth commandment).

frames.aligns: Characters grow toward goodness; love of friends and neighbors. Grade reason: growth theme fits; holiness and peace concerns.
frames.concerns: Fighting as delight (strong peace emphasis in the UMC); drinking (historic abstinence); sexual humor.

frames.aligns: Redemption, loyalty, self-sacrifice; fantasy has deep Anglican roots. Grade reason: broad fit; content judged case by case.
frames.concerns: Sexual gags and nudity; many gods.

frames.aligns: Mercy to defeated enemies; Goku's refusal to kill when unnecessary. Grade reason: violence as joy conflicts with nonresistance throughout.
frames.concerns: Fighting is the story's core pleasure and solution; tournaments and battles as heroism; sexual gags. Many conservative families avoid such media; Mennonite Church USA families may be more open.

frames.aligns: Family lineage, fathers protecting children, effort and self-improvement. Grade reason: early volumes touch several youth standards.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth warns against media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent"; sexual gags and nudity (vols. 1-16); drinking (Word of Wisdom). Z volumes may weigh less on modesty.

frames.aligns: Redemption over punishment; multi-species friendships; a woman scientist. Grade reason: themes fit; harassment and caricature concerns.
frames.concerns: Sexual harassment as comedy (Roshi); Mr. Popo's design; mockery of a gay-coded villain; violence as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah-like turning of former enemies; protecting life; loyalty. Grade reason: themes fit; views vary across movements.
frames.concerns: Gods as characters (idolatry, in Orthodox reading); tzniut concerns in the early gags (stronger in Orthodoxy, lighter in Reform).

frames.aligns: Discipline, striving, protecting the weak, humility in victory. Grade reason: shirk and haya concerns throughout.
frames.concerns: Many gods shown as real (shirk); nudity and immodest gags (haya); resurrection by wish; drinking.

frames.aligns: Righteous fighting to protect the world (dharma); karma-like consequences; rebirth of Buu as Uub; many deities fit a pluralistic view. Grade reason: cosmology resonates; modesty and ahimsa questions.
frames.concerns: Gods out-powered or joked about may feel disrespectful to some; lechery gags; violence as joy rather than duty.

frames.aligns: King Yama (Enma) judging souls; rebirth of Buu as Uub; Goku's orange dōgi echoes Buddhist monks (Toriyama). Grade reason: imagery resonates; precepts are strained.
frames.concerns: Endless craving for power and fights (tanha); violence as delight (first precept); lust gags (third precept); drinking (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Bulma as a scientist and leader; redemption over punishment; multinational, multi-species friendships. Grade reason: themes fit; harassment, race and LGBTQ portrayals concern.
frames.concerns: Roshi's harassment as comedy (ScreenWise flags it); Mr. Popo's design; mocking of a gay-coded villain; violence as the main solution (Common Sense Media).

frames.aligns: Human effort, not divine help, decides outcomes; reason and invention (Bulma); gods are characters, not truths. Grade reason: effort-centered humanism with consent concerns.
frames.concerns: Exploitative gags and lack of consent (ch. 2, 4); glorified violence.

frames.aligns: Effort, family lineage, fathers who protect, honor, loyalty, marriage and children. Grade reason: values fit; crude humor and absent father concern.
frames.concerns: Absent father; mother as comic nag; crude humor and nudity; violence level. Plugged In compares Z to "video sugar."

At 28, unsure of her sexuality and starved of touch, she books a session with a female sex worker to lose her virginity. The book follows what led there and what she learned about herself afterward.

entry.title: Innocent
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: A historical drama loosely based on the real Sanson family, hereditary executioners of Paris before the French Revolution. Gentle Charles-Henri Sanson recoils from the killing his inherited office demands but accepts it to protect his family, vowing to be the last executioner. His younger sister Marie-Joseph rebels against the gender rules of her time and seeks a place in the executions and at court.
entry.life_message: It holds up refusing to let birth, office or society dictate who you are, even at great personal cost.

entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: As a chubby child, Masamune Makabe was cruelly rejected by wealthy Aki Adagaki and nicknamed 'Pig's Foot'. Years later, slim, handsome and vain under a new surname, he plots to make Aki fall for him and then humiliate her. It emerges that Aki's maid Yoshino, jealous at the time, disguised herself as Aki and delivered the rejection, and the revenge plot unravels as the misunderstanding comes to light.

entry.premise: Worm-like Parasites arrive on Earth and take over human brains, then feed on other humans. One fails to reach 17-year-old Shinichi Izumi's brain and instead takes over his right hand, becoming Migi; the two keep separate minds and must cooperate to survive attacks from other Parasites. The series uses this to ask what makes us human and whether humanity has any right to moral superiority over other species.

entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Satoru Fujinuma, a 29-year-old struggling manga artist, has 'Revival', which throws him back moments before a disaster. When his mother is murdered, he is sent back to 1988 as an 11-year-old in Hokkaido, where he works to save her and to stop a serial killer targeting his classmates, including Kayo, who is beaten at home. The killer is his teacher Yashiro, who nearly drowns him; Satoru wakes from a 15-year coma and finally confronts him.
entry.life_message: It holds up courage to protect the vulnerable and loyal friendship that refuses to give up on others.

entry.title: Ashita no Joe: Fighting for Tomorrow
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Joe Yabuki, a drifter in Tokyo's San'ya slums, is taken up by alcoholic ex-trainer Danpei Tange and learns boxing, partly in juvenile detention, where he meets his rival Rikiishi. Rikiishi dies after their pro bout, and Joe struggles back to fight world champion José Mendoza, ending slumped in his corner, smiling, after fifteen rounds.
